title: All that glitters
caption: The globular cluster Messier 92, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 92 · constellation Hercules · about 25000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble captures Messier 92, a glittering globular cluster in the northern constellation of Hercules. A globular cluster is a ball of stars that orbits the core of a galaxy like a satellite, and this one is tightly packed with some 330 000 stars.

Among the Milky Way's globular clusters, Messier 92 ranks as one of the brightest, and under good conditions it can be seen with the naked eye. Like other globulars, it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium with only traces of anything else. It is classed as an Oosterhoff type II cluster, one of a family of clusters poor in metals, which is astronomers' term for every element beyond hydrogen and helium.

Studying the make-up of clusters like this helps astronomers work out their ages. Messier 92 turns out to be one of the oldest star clusters in our galaxy, with an age almost the same as that of the Universe.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.47 x 3.41 arcminutes) and distance (25000 light years), the frame spans roughly 25 × 25 light-years. Its light set out about 25,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Messier 92 can be seen with the naked eye under good conditions, but the eye cannot separate its stars as Hubble does, and part of Hubble's data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: Astronomer Johann Elert Bode discovered the cluster in 1777. Gilles Chapdelaine submitted a version of this picture to the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.
alt: A dense, bright ball of tightly packed stars.
